strengths: The paper offers a useful empirical perspective on multilingual visual supervision: captions originally produced in different languages may contribute complementary information even after translation into English. This is relevant to dataset construction and caption evaluation without requiring a new architecture or benchmark-leading performance.

The proposed comparison uses the same images and equally sized caption sets, addressing important image-content and annotation-count confounders. Crossmodal’s consistent annotation instructions and the investigation of both human captions and two captioning models strengthen the design.

The Visual Genome experiment provides evidence beyond unverified graph expansion. Table 3 reports object coverage increasing from 9.6% to 11.7% for Vertex and from 9.5% to 12.0% for LLaVA when replacing three English captions with English–French–Chinese captions.

The translation audit and additional human captioning study provide useful corroboration. Fifteen bilingual evaluators report high translation quality, while the study with 20 English/Japanese speakers on 30 images independently finds increased multilingual concept coverage. The qualitative examples make complementary background information understandable.
weaknesses: Quantitative reporting contains consequential inconsistencies. Every entry in Table 14’s 6×6 LLaVA fine-tuning matrix exactly matches the corresponding subset of Table 4’s Vertex matrix, although these are presented as separate experiments. Table 2 reports a Vertex monolingual attribute average of 1.98, exceeding every constituent value; their mean is approximately 1.69. These discrepancies undermine confidence in the claimed replication and aggregate effect sizes.

The central semantic measurement pipeline is insufficiently validated. Accuracy of the FLAN-T5 scene-graph parser on these captions is not reported, and the WordNet/embedding canonicalization lacks specified thresholds or sensitivity analysis. There is also no analysis controlling for caption length or verbosity. Visual Genome object coverage supports additional grounded objects, but does not establish the accuracy of added relations and attributes or quantify hallucination rates.

The expressive claims have weaker support than the object-coverage findings. LIWC authenticity, clout, and tone are measured on short English translations without validating that these scores preserve the original captions’ expressive properties. The translation audit evaluates factual categories rather than expressive fidelity. A source-language classifier achieving 16.43% accuracy versus 14.29% chance cannot establish that translation artifacts are absent.

Section 3.2’s argument against language-specific model modes is not justified. Similar diversity between multilingual outputs of one model and English outputs of several models does not distinguish mechanisms: no established relationship requires between-model diversity to exceed between-language diversity. The human comparisons likewise establish associations with language groups, while language, annotator population, and cultural background remain intertwined.

The fine-tuning results support adaptation to reference-caption distributions, but do not directly demonstrate improved visual representations. Some summaries also overstate the tables: Table 10 identifies multilingual training as best on mixed evaluation, whereas French-only training scores higher in Tables 4 and 15 (0.246 versus 0.244, and 0.154 versus 0.151). Table 15’s Chinese evaluation also contradicts a universal same-language advantage.

Reproducibility and uncertainty reporting are incomplete. Exact model checkpoints, decoding settings, fine-tuning hyperparameters, and split seeds are missing, and the principal coverage and fine-tuning tables lack confidence intervals or run variability. The descriptive finding is promising, but unresolved measurement validation and quantitative reliability currently outweigh the case for acceptance.
